'''Patrick Colonel Suppes''' ({{IPAc-en|ˈ|s|uː|p|iː|z}};<ref>[https://philosophy.stanford.edu/news/pat-suppes-obituary-new-york-times#:~:text=Suppes%20(pronounced%20SUE%2Dpeas),as%20his%20Harvard%20contemporary%20W.%20V. "Pat Suppes obituary from the New York Times"]: "pronounced SUE-peas"</ref> March 17, 1922 – November 17, 2014) was an American [[philosopher]] who made significant contributions to [[philosophy of science]], the theory of [[measurement]], the foundations of [[quantum mechanics]], [[decision theory]], [[psychology]] and [[educational technology]]. He was the Lucie Stern Professor of Philosophy Emeritus at [[Stanford University]] and until January 2010 was the Director of the [[Education Program for Gifted Youth]] also at Stanford.

== Early life and career ==
Suppes was born on March 17, 1922, in [[Tulsa, Oklahoma]]. He grew up as an only child, later with a half-brother George nearly 20 years his junior who was born in 1943 after Patrick had entered the army. His grandfather, C. E. Suppes, had moved to Oklahoma from Ohio. Suppes' father and grandfather were independent oil men. His mother died when he was a young boy. He was raised by his stepmother, who married his father when he was almost six years old. His parents did not have much formal education.<ref name="SAB">Cf. Suppes autobiography</ref>

Suppes began college at the [[University of Oklahoma]] in 1939, but transferred to the [[University of Chicago]] in his second year, citing boredom with intellectual life in Oklahoma as his primary motivation. In his third year, at the insistence of his family, Suppes attended the [[University of Tulsa]], majoring in [[physics]], before entering the [[Army Reserves]] in 1942. In 1943 he returned to the University of Chicago and graduated with a B.S. in [[meteorology]], and was stationed shortly thereafter at the [[Solomon Islands]] to serve during [[World War II]].<ref name="SAB"/>

Suppes was discharged from the [[United States Army Air Forces|Army Air Force]] in 1946.<ref name="SAB"/> In January 1947 he entered [[Columbia University]] as a graduate student in philosophy as a student of [[Ernest Nagel]] and received a [[Doctor of Philosophy|PhD]] in 1950.<ref name="SAB"/> In 1952 he went to [[Stanford University]], and from 1959 to 1992 he was the director of the [[Institute for Mathematical Studies in the Social Sciences]] (IMSSS). He subsequently became the Lucie Stern Professor of Philosophy, emeritus, at Stanford.

== Work ==

=== Computer-aided learning ===
In the 1960s Suppes and [[Richard C. Atkinson]] (the future president of the [[University of California]]) conducted experiments in using computers to teach math and reading to school children in the [[Palo Alto, California|Palo Alto]] area.<ref name="Pelfrey_Page21">{{cite book |last1=Pelfrey |first1=Patricia A. |title=Entrepreneurial President: Richard Atkinson and the University of California, 1995–2003 |date=2012 |publisher=University of California Press |location=Berkeley |isbn=978-0-520-95221-8 |page=21 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=j3yqEtmUPXsC&pg=PA21 |access-date=14 October 2020}}</ref> Stanford's [[Education Program for Gifted Youth]] and Computer Curriculum Corporation (CCC, now named Pearson Education Technologies) are indirect descendants of those early experiments.<ref>Kulik, James A., [https://www.nsf.gov/statistics/infbrief/nsf03301/ "School Mathematics and Science Programs Benefit From Instructional Technology"] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160307131803/http://www.nsf.gov/statistics/infbrief/nsf03301/ |date=2016-03-07 }}, NSF Info Brief, NSF 03-301, November 2002.</ref> At Stanford, Suppes was instrumental in encouraging the development of high-technology companies that were springing up in the field of educational software up into the 1990s, (such as [[Bien Logic]]).

One computer used in Suppes and Atkinson's Computer-assisted Instruction (CAI) experiments was the specialized [[IBM 1500]] Instructional System. Seeded by a research grant in 1964 from the U.S. Department of Education to the Institute for Mathematical Studies in the Social Sciences at Stanford University, the IBM 1500 CAI system was initially prototyped at the Brentwood Elementary School (Ravenswood City School District) in [[East Palo Alto, California]] by Suppes. The students first used the system in 1966.<ref>Suppes, Patrick,
[http://suppes-corpus.stanford.edu/techreports/IMSSS_174.pdf "Computer-assisted Instruction at Stanford"] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100717203424/http://suppes-corpus.stanford.edu/techreports/IMSSS_174.pdf |date=2010-07-17 }}, Technical Report No.174, May 19, 1971, Psychology and Education series, Institute for Mathematical Studies in the Social Sciences, Stanford University</ref><ref name="Hunka1996">Hunka, Stephen; Buck, George (1996) [http://www.quasar.ualberta.ca/edmedia/readingsnc/Hunkabuck.pdf "The Rise and Fall of CAI at the University of Alberta's Faculty of Education"] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110608020235/http://www.quasar.ualberta.ca/edmedia/readingsnc/Hunkabuck.pdf |date=2011-06-08 }}. Canadian Journal of Educational Communication, 21(2), 153–170. (also: [http://www.cjlt.ca/index.php/cjlt/issue/view/45 full journal issue])</ref>

Suppes' Dial-a-Drill program was a touchtone phone interface for CAI. Ten schools around Manhattan were involved in the program which delivered three lessons per week by telephone.<ref>{{Cite news|title=Learning by phone|date=March 8, 1969|work=New York Amsterdam News|page=9}}</ref> Dial-a-Drill adjusted the routine for students who answered two questions incorrectly.<ref>{{Cite book|title=The management of education: A systematic design for educational revolution|last=Umans|first=S|publisher=Doubleday|year=1970|location=Garden City, N.Y}}</ref> The system went online in March 1969. Touchtone telephones were installed in the homes of children participating in the program. Field workers educated parents on the benefits of the program and collected feedback.<ref>{{Cite book|title=Final Report: An Evaluation of the Dial-A-Drill Program|last1=Beech|first1=R. P|last2=McClelland|first2=S. D|last3=Horowitz|first3=G. R|last4=Forlano|first4=G|publisher=Center for Field Research and School|year=1970|location=New York University}}</ref>

=== Decision theory ===
During the 1950s and 1960s Suppes collaborated with [[Donald Davidson (philosopher)|Donald Davidson]] on [[decision theory]], at Stanford. Their initial work followed lines of thinking which had been anticipated in 1926 by [[Frank P. Ramsey]], and involved experimental testing of their theories, culminating in the 1957 monograph ''[[Decision Making: An Experimental Approach]]''. Such commentators as [[Kirk Ludwig]] trace the origins of Davidson's theory of [[radical interpretation]] to his formative work with Suppes.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://catdir.loc.gov/catdir/samples/cam033/2002035082.pdf|title=Donald Davidson|editor=Kirk Ludwig|website=Catdir.loc.gov|access-date=27 October 2021}}</ref>

== Awards and honors ==
* He was elected to the [[American Academy of Arts and Sciences]] in 1968.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Patrick Suppes |url=https://www.amacad.org/person/patrick-suppes |access-date=2022-04-14 |website=American Academy of Arts & Sciences |language=en}}</ref>
* In 1971 he was elected as a Permanent Member of the Institut international de philosophie.
* In 1978 he was elected as a member of the [[National Academy of Sciences]] for his work on mathematical psychology.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Patrick Suppes |url=https://www.nasonline.org/directory-entry/patrick-suppes-brav3x/ |access-date=2022-04-14 |website=www.nasonline.org}}</ref>
* On November 13, 1990, President [[George H. W. Bush]] awarded Suppes with the President's [[National Medal of Science]] for work in Behavioral and Social Science.<ref>[https://www.nsf.gov/od/nms/recip_details.cfm?recip_id=353 National Medal of Science page] ({{webarchive |url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070311051543/https://www.nsf.gov/od/nms/recip_details.cfm?recip_id=353 |date=March 11, 2007 }}) Citation: "For his broad efforts to deepen the theoretical and empirical understanding of four major areas: the measurement of subjective probability and utility in uncertain situations; the development and testing of general learning theory; the semantics and syntax of natural language; and the use of interactive computer programs for instruction."</ref>
* He was elected to the [[American Philosophical Society]] in 1991.<ref>{{Cite web |title=APS Member History |url=https://search.amphilsoc.org/memhist/search?creator=Patrick+Suppes&title=&subject=&subdiv=&mem=&year=&year-max=&dead=&keyword=&smode=advanced |access-date=2022-04-14 |website=search.amphilsoc.org}}</ref>
* In 1994 he was inducted as a [[Fellow]] of the [[Association for Computing Machinery]]. He is the laureate of the 2003 [[Lakatos Award]] for his contributions to the philosophy of science.
* He was a member of the [[Norwegian Academy of Science and Letters]].<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.dnva.no/c26849/artikkel/vis.html?tid=40104|title=Gruppe 3: Idéfag|publisher=[[Norwegian Academy of Science and Letters]]|language=no|access-date=16 January 2011|archive-date=27 September 2011|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110927171625/http://www.dnva.no/c26849/artikkel/vis.html?tid=40104|url-status=dead}}</ref>
* In 2012, he was given the first ever [[Software and Information Industry Association]] Lifetime Achievement Award<ref>{{cite web|url=http://archive.siia.net/index.php?option=com_content&view=article&id=1071:siia-honors-education-industry-veterans-with-prestigious-awards&catid=62:press-room-overview&Itemid=507|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160911224319/http://archive.siia.net/index.php?option=com_content&view=article&id=1071:siia-honors-education-industry-veterans-with-prestigious-awards&catid=62:press-room-overview&Itemid=507|url-status=dead|archive-date=September 11, 2016|title=SIIA Honors Education Industry Veterans with Prestigious Awards|publisher=SIIA|language=en|access-date=7 September 2016}}</ref>
